activity_context.topic_title: Phase Portraits for Linear Systems With Complex Eigenvalues

examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Parameters of a System Given Its Phase Portrait
examples.problem:
The phase portrait for a system of linear differential equations whose matrix has two complex eigenvalues $\lambda = a \pm b\text{i}$ is shown above. Provide an interpretation of the portrait and determine the possible values of $a.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/6d13d0dfadac45d40b74cb7e740a880305098f0939e2f45d74706c4022183c54.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},$ where $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = a + b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is unbounded, representing a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise. Thus, we must have $a \neq 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward the origin.

Hence, to insure that $e^{at} \to 0,$ we require $a < 0.$

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $-0.71$ | $-1$ |
| $y$ | $5$ | $3.54$ | $0$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1$ and $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1.$ Thus, the obtained curve is $\text{bounded}.$ So, we have $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$
